# Independent audit: disjoint proper-cap partitions



Source: `candidate ed1a79b6ef1fd236`.


dedicated verifier for this general incidence statement. The proof's
partition and no-whole-positive-fiber hypotheses are essential to its
present scope; no full-fiber or fractional-cover extension is imported.

## 1. Intrinsic measure and positive fibers

The finite disjoint union of compact convex integer fibers has
Hausdorff dimension equal to their maximum affine dimension q. When
q>=1, precisely the q-dimensional fibers contribute finite positive
H_q mass; the others contribute zero. Translation from a fiber into
its continuous affine plane is an isometry, so the fiber sum uses the
stated normalized Hausdorff measure with no extra factors.

Global null overlaps and an almost-everywhere cover imply the same
properties on every positive fiber individually, because there are
finitely many fibers and every summand is nonnegative. Restricting an
ambient halfspace to a fiber plane gives a proper halfspace, the whole
plane, or the empty set. The full-plane alternative is excluded by
Assumption 3; empty or null traces can be ignored in the local lemma.

The positive base set P is also lattice-complete, although this fact
is not needed by the proof: if an integer h is a convex combination
of points of P, its actual fiber contains the corresponding Minkowski
combination of q-dimensional bodies. The latter has dimension at
least q and hence exactly q, because no integer fiber has larger
dimension. It has positive intrinsic q-volume, so h belongs to P.
Only positively weighted summands are used in this argument.

## 2. Local two-cap partition lemma

A finite closed cover up to null mass is an actual cover of the whole
convex body. Indeed an omitted point would have a relatively open
neighborhood disjoint from the closed union, and every such body
neighborhood contains positive interior volume. A positive proper
halfspace trace has its boundary intersecting the body's interior.

At an interior point of that cutting hyperplane, another cap cannot
contain the point strictly: it would overlap the first cap on a
positive-volume one-sided neighborhood. Points approaching from the
other side are covered by other caps. Finiteness gives a subsequence
in one cap; closedness and the preceding strict-containment exclusion
put the limiting point on that cap's boundary. Thus the relatively
open part of the first cutting hyperplane is covered by the finite
union of the other cutting hyperplanes.

In dimension at least two a finite union of proper lower-dimensional
affine intersections cannot cover this relatively open set. In
dimension one the section is a single point and some other boundary
must be that same point. Thus two hyperplanes coincide. Equal
orientation would produce positive overlap, so their orientations
are opposite. These two caps cover the entire affine plane, and any
third positive trace would overlap at least one in positive volume.
This proves exactly two positive traces, including the one-dimensional
case and nonsmooth bodies.

## 3. Midpoint label preservation

For each positive fiber choose a point in the relative interior of
the common two-cap section. It lies in the relative interior of the
fiber. Both selected cap margins are zero. Every other cap margin
is strictly negative: a nonzero intrinsic normal through an interior
point cuts positive volume, while a zero intrinsic normal with zero
margin would include the entire fiber. Thus neither can have a null
trace and margin zero at this marked point.

For same-parity bases z,w, their midpoint h is an actual integer base.
The Minkowski midpoint lies in K_h. Its affine direction is the sum
of the two q-dimensional source directions, so dimension at most q
forces the directions to coincide. The target also has dimension q
and the same direction. Its affine plane is the midpoint of the two
source affine planes. Intrinsic balls about the marked source points
therefore give an intrinsic ball about their midpoint inside K_h.

Every ambient cap margin at that midpoint is the average of its
source margins. It is zero exactly on the intersection of the two
pair labels and strictly negative otherwise. Empty intersection
contradicts cover. A one-element intersection also contradicts cover:
all other caps stay strictly absent in a neighborhood, and the sole
remaining cap has a nonzero normal on the common q-direction space,
so its opposite half-neighborhood is uncovered with positive volume.
Both pair labels therefore agree. Both caps cut positive volume in
the midpoint fiber, and the local lemma identifies its label with
the same pair. No global parallelism across different components is
required.

This proof retains the full ambient affine margin throughout. It
does not shear the actual family or identify nonparallel fibers.
It also does not assume that each midpoint component is itself
lattice-complete.

## 4. Global cap count and strict component count

Every positive global cap has a positive trace on some positive
fiber, so appears in one of the component pair labels. Each component
supplies at most two indices. Hence r<=2c(P), even when labels on
different components share indices.

All points of any one occupied parity lie in the same component,
since each pair is joined with its midpoint. The resulting map from
occupied parities onto components proves c(P)<=k. If c(P)=k, this map
is bijective; each component has exactly one parity. Its point set
is then closed under every midpoint, which belongs to the same
component. A closest distinct pair would yield a distinct point at
half the minimum distance. Finiteness forces every component to be
a singleton, so |P|=k. The contrapositive gives c(P)<=k-1 when
|P|>k, and thus r<=2(k-1). There is no hidden assumption about affine
rank, ambient integer dimension, or general position.

With equal positive cap mass D, coverage and pairwise null overlaps
give the exact finite-measure identity M=rD. The bounds
D>=M/(2c(P))>=M/(2k) follow without any boundary correction. Since
Gamma_q<=1/2 for every q>=1, the comparison with Gamma_q M/k has
the correct direction and exact factor.

## 5. Closed boundaries, sharpness, and scope

Nonconstant cuts in a q-dimensional fiber have H_q-null hyperplane
boundaries. A cap constant on a positive fiber can instead carry
full boundary mass; the theorem excludes that case explicitly by
Assumption 3, rather than silently replacing closed halfspaces by
open ones. Lower-dimensional fibers are null in this theorem's
q>=1 measure and may be ignored for these measure conclusions.
The q=0 case is not asserted. In particular d=0 is outside the
hypotheses; n=0 remains valid.

In the sharpness example each binary base is in its own parity and
component. The affine isolation function ell_b is zero at its own
vertex and at least one at every other integer base. The strict
choice L>max_K |u.x| makes both associated caps empty on all other
fibers. On the own fiber, the two centrally symmetric through-center
cuts have mass V/2, partition the fiber up to null boundary, and are
proper. Therefore r=2^(n+1), M=2^n V, and D=M/(2k), including n=0.
All normals are legitimate nonzero ambient normals; no non-lattice
coordinate transformation occurs.

The final overlap warning is also correct: the three barycentric
vertex caps of a triangle at threshold 1/3 have area fraction 4/9,
cover the triangle, and overlap on regions of positive area. Equal
budgets do not imply the partition premise. Consequently the proved
result is an exact obstruction to sufficiently small equal-budget
*partitions*, not a numerical bound for arbitrary critical-cap covers
or a resolution of OC.
